title: What Language Awareness Means for Learners
brief: Define language awareness as it applies to the learner, drawing directly on the module's glossary definition: 'a focus on aspects of language within a given context; paying attention to or noticing the language detail in a context.' Explain the distinction the module makes between a holistic, top-down communicative focus on function versus the additional need to attend to form—grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation—within that same context. Use the module's list of language awareness characteristics to show what learner-side awareness looks like in practice: making conscious effort, reflecting analytically on language, and using meta-language to talk about what they notice. Emphasise the module's point that language awareness is more than a focus on form; it also includes the pragmatic, situational, and cultural use of that form in context.

title: Noticing Patterns: Inductive and Deductive Pathways
brief: Explain the two routes through which learners can build awareness of language patterns, using the module's definitions of inductive techniques (learners discover rules themselves through experience with the language) and deductive techniques (learners are taught rules and then apply them). Draw on the module's statement that language awareness involves 'a balance of inductive and deductive techniques to focus on specific aspects of language,' and connect this to the learner's active role: the module describes learners as 'more conscious participants in their own learning as they do the work of analyzing and reflecting on language and its use.' Use the module's description of conscious effort—'effort that learners make deliberately, knowing and understanding the purpose for the action'—to frame why noticing patterns is a skill learners must develop intentionally rather than passively absorb.

title: Guessing Meaning from Context: The Language Safari
brief: Walk learners through the Language Safari activity described in the module as a practical technique for developing the skill of guessing meaning from context. Explain the procedure as the module presents it: learners first write or explain the meaning of two or three vocabulary items before seeing the text, then read the text and search for those items, then answer the module's specific debrief questions—whether first definitions matched actual use, what clues the overall context and content provided, and how grammatical structures in the text gave additional clues. Use the module's sample text (the car-chase news story with the words 'run,' 'stop,' and 'coast') to illustrate concretely how a single word can appear as different parts of speech, as part of a phrasal verb, or as part of an idiom, and how context helps the learner resolve those multiple meanings.

title: Word Families, Collocation, and Multiple Meanings
brief: Focus on the vocabulary dimension of language awareness that the module highlights through its sample text and activity design: the fact that vocabulary items 'can occur as more than one part of speech in the text (verb, noun, etc.) or as part of a phrasal verb or idiom.' Use the module's worked example—'run' appearing four times, 'stop' three times, and 'coast' twice in the car-chase text—to show learners how a single base form generates a family of related uses and collocations (e.g., 'ran red lights,' 'ran out of gas,' 'coasted to a stop'). Connect this to the module's point about choosing vocabulary items that 'could have more than one meaning or use,' explaining why awareness of word families and collocational patterns helps learners move beyond single-definition memorization toward flexible, contextualized understanding. Also draw on the module's note that the Language Safari extension can use audio or video segments, reinforcing that pattern-noticing applies across modes.

title: Using Meta-Language to Talk About Language
brief: Explain meta-language as the module defines it—'language used by the teacher and students to talk about language or about learning strategies and techniques,' with examples such as verb, gerund, compound noun, present or past tense—and show why developing a meta-language is itself a learner skill. Draw on the module's Language Safari debrief question that asks learners to identify what meta-language they used when discussing the focus words, positioning this reflection as an awareness-raising act in its own right. Use the module's classroom example of the primary school skit to illustrate meta-language in action: the teacher and aide held up yellow sheets displaying target language ('How did you feel?', 'Alike or different?', 'Activities, chores') so that learners could see and name the language they were using. Connect to the module's point that the green planning sheet organised language explicitly by grammatical category—nouns for place and packing, verbs and phrases for activities—giving learners a visible framework for talking about how language works.

title: Awareness-Raising Activities: From Classroom to Action Plan
brief: Bring together the unit's themes by surveying the awareness-raising activity types the module describes and then presenting the module's four-step action plan as a model for learners developing their own awareness practice. Cover the skit activity (Across the Wide, Dark Sea) as an example of integrated-skills, contextualized language work in which vocabulary such as 'cold' and 'shivering' was reinforced through repetition and physical demonstration, and the travel-planning poster task in which authentic materials—travel brochures with pictures—allowed learners at different proficiency levels to access language and build vocabulary through real-world content. Explain the module's point that authentic sources are those 'used by native speakers or other users of the target language for real-world communication,' and that comprehensible input contains linguistic items 'slightly above the learner's competence.' Close by walking through the module's action-plan steps—choosing a topic, designing a contextualized lesson outline, sharing it for peer feedback, and revising it—as a transferable process learners and trainee teachers can use to keep building language awareness beyond any single activity.
